summary: Extends WebDAV to define a standard way of accessing, managing and sharing calendar and scheduling data in the iCalendar format. This document defines the calendar-access feature.

plainLanguage.summary: CalDAV is a set of rules for calendar applications to store and retrieve calendar data from a server. It builds on WebDAV and iCalendar so different clients can use the same calendar collections and reports.

subtitle: How calendar applications access and manage shared calendar data over WebDAV.

tldr.problem: Calendar access built on HTTP and WebDAV did not interoperate because implementations made different choices about storing calendar data and supporting calendar features.
tldr.mechanism: CalDAV models a calendar as a WebDAV collection of iCalendar resources and defines calendar properties, a calendar-creation method, reports, access control, and ETag rules.
tldr.outcome: Clients can create, retrieve, search, and synchronize calendar data using a shared model. RFC 4791 is a Proposed Standard updated by several later RFCs.

today: RFC 4791 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5689, RFC 6638, RFC 6764, RFC 7809, RFC 7953, and RFC 8996.

sections.title: What CalDAV Adds to WebDAV
sections.content:
Several companies had built calendar access using HTTP to upload and download iCalendar objects and WebDAV to list resources. Those implementations did not interoperate because they made different choices about how to model calendar data and add missing features.

RFC 4791 defines the calendar-access feature of CalDAV. A server advertising support must provide the required iCalendar, WebDAV, access-control, ETag, and calendaring-report features, and support transport over TLS. It advertises support with calendar-access in the DAV response header to an OPTIONS request.

The server must also advertise supported calendaring reports on calendar collections and calendar object resources. Support for the MKCALENDAR method is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar programs had used different rules to store data on WebDAV servers, so they could not reliably work together. CalDAV defines one shared model and the features a server must provide.

sections.title: Calendars as Collections of Resources
sections.content:
A CalDAV calendar is a WebDAV collection. Its direct child resources hold calendar objects, such as events, to-dos, and journal entries. The server is the canonical location for calendar data, so clients must be ready for changes made by other clients.

A calendar object resource cannot mix different component types, except for the VTIMEZONE components it needs. Components with different UIDs must be stored in separate resources; components with the same UID, such as a recurring event and its overridden instance, must be stored together.

A calendar collection contains calendar object resources and ordinary collections, but calendar collections cannot be nested inside one another. The collection's resource type identifies it as both a WebDAV collection and a CalDAV calendar.
sections.plainLanguage: A calendar is a server folder, and each calendar item is a resource inside it. A repeating event and its changed instances stay together in one resource.

sections.title: Properties That Describe a Calendar
sections.content:
CalDAV properties describe a calendar collection and can tell clients what the server accepts. Examples include a human-readable description, the calendar time zone, supported component and data types, and limits on resource size, dates, recurrence instances, or attendees.

The calendar time zone helps the server interpret dates and floating times when it checks a query's time range or creates a free-busy response. If the server defines supported component or data types, attempts to store unlisted types fail. Without a supported-data property, the server accepts only text/calendar with iCalendar version 2.0.

The calendar-home-set property on a user's principal identifies collections that contain that user's calendars. The read-free-busy privilege allows another user to see busy times without seeing event details.
sections.plainLanguage: A calendar's properties describe its time zone and what data or sizes it accepts. A home-set property helps a client find a user's calendars, while a separate permission can reveal busy times without revealing event details.

sections.title: Creating Calendars and Calendar Items
sections.content:
The MKCALENDAR method creates a calendar collection. Servers are encouraged to support it, but the RFC only recommends it because some services create one calendar for each user in advance. A request can set collection properties, and if it fails, the server must restore its previous state.

Clients create or replace calendar object resources with HTTP PUT. Conditional request headers such as If-None-Match and If-Match help distinguish a new resource from an update. The server checks requirements such as valid calendar data, supported components, UID rules, and any collection limits.

Every calendar object resource must have a strong ETag, which clients can use to detect changes. A server should return a strong ETag after PUT when it stored exactly the bytes the client sent.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the server to create a calendar, then upload each calendar item as a resource. The server gives each item a version tag so clients can tell when it changes.

sections.title: Querying Calendars with Reports
sections.content:
CalDAV servers must support calendaring reports. calendar-query searches for resources that match a filter. A filter can select component types, properties, text, or a time range. For a time range, the server must expand recurring components to check whether any instance overlaps it.

calendar-multiget retrieves specific calendar resources named by their URLs. free-busy-query takes one time range and returns a VFREEBUSY component containing busy periods for resources the user may read or may read free-busy for. A reader can infer free time from those busy periods.

Servers must support substring matching with the i;ascii-casemap and i;octet collations. They may support others and advertise which ones are available.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask for calendar items matching a time or property filter, fetch a named list of items, or ask when a user is busy. For recurring events, the server checks whether any occurrence falls in the requested time.

sections.title: Synchronizing Calendar Changes
sections.content:
CalDAV clients can cache each resource's URL, ETag, and calendar data. To synchronize a time range, a client can ask for the resources and their ETags, compare them with its cache, and fetch new or changed resources with calendar-multiget. The client must also track creations and deletions to reconcile both copies.

Clients can limit queries to the time span currently shown, or synchronize the present and near future first. This reduces the amount of data transferred and processed.

Changing a calendar object resource requires replacing the entire resource with PUT; the RFC does not define incremental changes to individual properties. WebDAV locks can help prevent conflicting edits.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can compare each item's ETag with its saved copy and fetch only items that changed. It can focus on the dates a person is viewing instead of downloading the entire calendar.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
HTTP traffic is sent in the clear unless protected. HTTP Basic authentication MUST NOT be used unless TLS is active. Servers must also guard against reports that consume excessive CPU, memory, or disk; a request to expand a very large recurring event is one example.

Clients must choose resource names that do not reveal information in the calendar data or the nature of a collection. Free-busy responses can reveal whether a user has multiple events, so servers should combine adjacent or overlapping busy periods of the same type.

Procedure alarms can be a security risk. Clients and servers are not required to execute them.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects calendar traffic, and Basic authentication must not be used without it. Servers should limit expensive queries, and resource names and free-busy results should avoid revealing private details.
